w-b-yeats: William Butler Yeats was born in Sandymount, County Dublin, on 13 June 1865, a Protestant of Anglo-Irish descent. His father, John, studied law and became a portrait painter. His mother, Susan Mary Pollexfen, came from a wealthy merchant family in Sligo, and the family soon moved to Merville in Sligo, which he came to think of as his spiritual home. He was educated in Dublin and London, and began writing at seventeen, drawing heavily on Shelley, Spenser and pre-Raphaelite verse before turning to Irish mythology, folklore and Blake.

His first collection, The Wanderings of Oisin and Other Poems, appeared in 1889. He had a lifelong interest in mysticism, spiritualism and the occult. In 1889 he met Maud Gonne, an ardent Irish nationalist, and his unrequited love for her had a lasting effect on his poetry. She refused his proposals in 1891, 1899, 1900 and 1901 and in 1903 married Major John MacBride. In 1899 Yeats, Lady Gregory, Edward Martyn and George Moore founded the Irish Literary Theatre, and with Lady Gregory and John Millington Synge he founded the Abbey Theatre, serving as its chief in its early years. His plays include Cathleen ni Houlihan (1902).

From 1900 his poetry became more rooted in the physical world, realistic and political. Collections of this phase include The Wild Swans at Coole (1919) and The Tower (1928). In 1922 he was appointed to the first Senate of the Irish Free State, and he served a second term from 1925. In December 1923 he received the Nobel Prize in Literature for poetry that gives expression to the spirit of a whole nation, and the money allowed him to repay his own debts and his father's. In the 1930s he composed marching songs for the Blueshirts, never used, and later distanced himself from the movement.

Yeats died of heart failure at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, France, on 28 January 1939, aged 73. He had wished to be buried quickly in France and moved to Sligo a year later. In September 1948 his body was taken to the churchyard of St Columba's Church at Drumcliff, County Sligo, aboard the Irish Naval Service corvette LÉ Macha. His epitaph comes from the last lines of Under Ben Bulben.
wales: Wales is a generally mountainous country on the western side of central southern Great Britain, about 270 kilometres from north to south. It is bordered by England to the east and by sea in all other directions, with about 2,700 kilometres of coastline. The highest mountains are in Snowdonia, where Snowdon (Yr Wyddfa) rises to 1,085 metres. The English words Wales and Welsh derive from an Old English word, Wealh, which the Anglo-Saxons used for the Britons; the Welsh name for themselves, Cymry, descends from a Brythonic word meaning 'fellow-countrymen'.

The territory was permanently settled from the end of the last ice age. In the Bronze Age the Great Orme in North Wales became Britain's premier producer of copper. After the Roman withdrawal, Britain fractured into kingdoms, and Anglo-Saxon settlers gradually displaced the culture and language of the Britons, leaving one group isolated in the western peninsula, whom their English neighbours called Welsh. Medieval Wales stayed divided into kingdoms that fought each other as much as the English.

In the 10th century Hywel ap Cadell, later Hywel Dda, gained control of Gwynedd and Powys in 942 and so of nearly all of Wales, and codified Welsh law. Wales was briefly united under Gruffudd ap Llywelyn in 1055. Owain Glyndŵr led the Welsh Revolt in the early 15th century and briefly re-established an independent state with its own parliament. In the 19th century mining and metallurgy transformed Wales into an industrial society, and the population rose from 587,000 in 1801 to 2,421,000 by 1911.

Both Welsh and English are official languages, and Welsh is dominant in parts of the north and west. Wales has four UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Castles and Town Walls of King Edward I in Gwynedd, the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct and Canal, the Blaenavon Industrial Landscape and the Slate Landscape of Northwest Wales. Medieval Welsh manuscripts such as the Red Book of Hergest preserve the Mabinogion and the earliest forms of the Arthurian legend.
wallonia: Wallonia is one of the three regions of Belgium, with Flanders and Brussels. It is landlocked, covers 16,901 square kilometres, 55 per cent of the country's area, and holds about 31 per cent of its people. Most of its major cities and two thirds of its population lie in the east to west valley of the Sambre and Meuse, the former industrial backbone of Belgium. To the north of the valley lies the fertile Central Belgian Plateau, and the south and south-east form the forested highlands of the Ardennes. Its largest city is Charleroi and its capital is Namur.

Julius Caesar conquered Gaul in 57 BCE, and the Low Countries became part of the province of Gallia Belgica. Its people were Celtic with a Germanic influence that was stronger in the north. They became Gallo-Romans, whom their Germanic neighbours called Walha, and they gave up their Celtic dialects for Vulgar Latin. The Sambre and Meuse valley was already an important industrial area in the Roman Empire.

In the Middle Ages the region was a centre of brass and bronze working, with Huy, Dinant and Chimay as important towns, and Mosan art, a regional Romanesque style, flourished in the Meuse valley in the 11th to 13th centuries. In the 12th and 13th centuries the iron masters of Liège developed a way of refining iron ore with a blast furnace, called the Walloon Method.

Wallonia was the first fully industrialised area in continental Europe, in the 19th century, and was second only to the United Kingdom in industrialisation. The coal and iron valley from Liège to Charleroi became known as the sillon industriel. Strikes and general strikes took place there, among them the Walloon jacquerie of 1886 and the general strikes of 1893, 1902 and 1913, the last for universal suffrage. After the Second World War a general strike of 1950 was directed against Leopold III and the winter general strike of 1960 to 1961 demanded autonomy for Wallonia.

Belgium is a federal state, and the Walloon Region is governed by the Parliament of Wallonia and the Government of Wallonia. The first regional council sat on 15 October 1980, and a directly elected parliament was created in June 1995. French is the official language, and German also in the eastern cantons annexed from the German Empire at the end of the First World War. Traditional regional Romance languages such as Walloon and Picard are in decline. In 1995 Walloon Brabant became the youngest of its five provinces.
warli: Until the 1870s the Warli were the primary owners of all land in the Umbergaon, Dhanu and Palghar talukas of the Thane district. In that decade the British colonial administration brought their territories under direct control, and outsiders, among them Mahajans and petty officers, used the Warlis' illiteracy to take their lands. The Warli became labourers on land they had owned. Under the begar system they cultivated the landlords' holdings without pay; as sharecroppers on small plots of inferior land they surrendered at least half the produce. Records of the period document public whippings, torture and the sexual oppression of Warli women.

In 1939 an inquiry by the British magistrate David Symington found that their living conditions had reached an abysmal depth. Organised resistance followed, led by Shamrao and Godavari Parulekar. In May 1945 about 5,000 Warlis gathered at Zari and pledged to end the begar system. In October 1945 police fired on a rally of 7,000 people at Talwada, killing five activists, among them the leader Jethya Gangad. The begar system was abolished and minimum wages were established, and by the early 1950s most of the feudal exactions had ended.

The Warli speak Varli, an unwritten language of the southern zone of the Indo-Aryan languages. They have animistic beliefs of their own and have also adopted many Hindu beliefs. Traditionally semi-nomadic, living in small groups led by a headman, they are today mainly agriculturists who grow rice and wheat among other crops. Married women wear toe rings and necklaces, and some Warli practise polygyny.

Their ritual paintings are made inside the huts, for occasions such as weddings and harvests, in white rice paste on walls of branches, earth and cow dung, with a bamboo stick chewed at the end as a brush. At the centre stands a square, the chauk, which in one type encloses the mother goddess Palaghata, symbol of fertility; around it are scenes of hunting, fishing, farming and dancing. Human and animal bodies are drawn as two triangles joined at the tip.

Painting was the preserve of Warli women until the late 1970s. In that decade Jivya Soma Mashe and his son Balu Mashe began to paint outside any ritual, as an artistic pursuit of their own. The writer Yashodhara Dalmia, in The Painted World of the Warlis, claimed that the tradition reaches back to 2500 or 3000 BCE.
warsaw: Warsaw lies in east-central Poland on both banks of the Vistula, in the heartland of the Masovian Plain, about 260 km from the Baltic Sea and 523 km east of Berlin. The name in Polish is Warszawa, and its origin is uncertain. One hypothesis reads it as belonging to Warsz, a short form of the Old Polish name Warcisław, and the original Warszawa was a small fishing settlement on the river bank. Folk etymology tells of the fisherman Wars and the mermaid Sawa, who lived in the Vistula.

The first fortified settlements on the site were at Bródno in the 9th or 10th century and at Jazdów in the 12th or 13th century. Bolesław II of Masovia, Prince of Płock, established the town in about 1300, and in 1413 it was officially made capital of the Masovian Duchy, when it had about 4,500 inhabitants. The city rose to prominence after 1596, when Sigismund III moved the Polish capital and royal court from Kraków. By the 18th century Warsaw had passed Gdańsk as the most populous city of Poland. It was the capital of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth until 1795 and afterwards the seat of Napoleon's Duchy of Warsaw.

The 19th century and the Industrial Revolution made it one of the largest and most densely populated cities in Europe. Before the Second World War it held the world's second-largest Jewish population after New York, about 30 percent of its people in the late 1930s. The city was bombed and besieged in 1939. Much of the historic city was destroyed and its diverse population decimated by the Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Warsaw Uprising of 1944 and systematic razing.

Warsaw is the capital and most populous city of Poland, with about 1.87 million residents, and the seat of both houses of the Polish Parliament. The reconstructed Old Town was listed as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1980. Other landmarks are the Royal Castle, Sigismund's Column and Wilanów Palace.
washington-dc: Washington, D.C., lies in the Mid-Atlantic region of the East Coast, on the northeast bank of the Potomac River, across from Virginia and surrounded by Maryland to the north, east and south. The south bank of the Potomac forms the border with Virginia, and the Anacostia River and Rock Creek are its two major tributaries. The Chesapeake and Ohio Canal starts in Georgetown and was used in the 19th century to bypass the Little Falls of the Potomac. The district was named for Columbia, the female personification of the American nation, and the name Washington was added later, from George Washington, the first president.

The Algonquian-speaking Piscataway people inhabited the area when Europeans arrived in the early 17th century, and the Nacotchtank maintained settlements around the Anacostia River. Conflicts with colonists and neighbouring tribes displaced the Piscataway, some of whom founded a new settlement near Point of Rocks, Maryland, in 1699. The Constitution of 1789 called for a federal district under the exclusive jurisdiction of Congress. The Residence Act, adopted on 16 July 1790, approved a capital district along the Potomac and is considered the city's founding date. In 1800 the capital moved from Philadelphia, Congress began meeting in the unfinished Capitol, and President John Adams moved into the White House.

In 1791 President George Washington commissioned the French-born military engineer Pierre Charles L'Enfant to design the capital. His plan featured broad avenues radiating out from rectangles, with a grand garden-lined avenue on the site of the National Mall, inspired by Versailles and the Tuileries. Washington dismissed L'Enfant in March 1792 after conflicts with the commissioners overseeing construction, and Andrew Ellicott completed the design. In 1846 Congress returned to Virginia the land it had ceded, including Alexandria, and in 1871 it made the entire district a single municipality.

Washington, D.C., is the capital of the United States and its only federal district, not part of any state. It houses the White House, the Capitol and the Supreme Court Building, and its National Mall holds the Jefferson Memorial, the Lincoln Memorial and the Washington Monument. Since the 1973 Home Rule Act it has had an elected mayor and a 13-member council, though Congress retains the power to overturn local laws. Its residents elect one non-voting delegate to the House of Representatives. Ford's Theatre, where Abraham Lincoln was shot on 14 April 1865, is both a theatre and a museum.
weimar: The oldest records of Weimar date to 899, and its name derives from Old High German words for holy and for standing water. It was the seat of the County of Weimar, first mentioned in 949, one of the most powerful jurisdictions in early medieval Thuringia, and fell to the Wettins after 1346. The Reformation was introduced in 1525, and Martin Luther stayed in the city several times. After the Ernestines lost the Schmalkaldic War in 1547 and Wittenberg passed to the Albertines, the ruler made Weimar his residence in 1552, and it remained one until the end of the monarchy in 1918.

The period from the regency of Anna Amalia, which began in 1758, through her son Carl August to Goethe's death in 1832 is called the golden or classical age. Goethe, Schiller, Herder, Wieland and Bertuch lived there. Goethe moved to Weimar in 1775 and served the Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach as Privy Councilor. A liberal Saxe-Weimar constitution came into effect in 1816. In 1842 Franz Liszt became the Grand Ducal court conductor and organised the premiere of Richard Wagner's Lohengrin in 1850. Friedrich Nietzsche moved to the city in 1897 and died there three years later.

The Weimar Republic's constitution was drafted in the city rather than in Berlin because the capital was considered too dangerous for the National Assembly after street rioting during the Spartacist uprising. Reich President Friedrich Ebert hoped the choice would remind the Allies of Weimar Classicism while they deliberated the Treaty of Versailles. Artists and architects including Walter Gropius, Wassily Kandinsky and Paul Klee founded the Bauhaus there. The Nazis held a party convention in Weimar in 1926, and the first concentration camps were set up near the city in 1933.

Weimar is a city in Thuringia, in central Germany between Erfurt and Jena, with a population of about 65,000. It was the capital of Thuringia until 1948. Two World Heritage Sites include buildings in the city: Classical Weimar, with 11 sites linked to the 18th and early 19th centuries, and the Bauhaus sites. The Bauhaus University, the Liszt School of Music and the Duchess Anna Amalia Library are among its institutions.
wellington: Wellington stands at the south-western tip of the North Island, between Cook Strait and the Remutaka Range. Steep hills shape and constrain much of the city. The Kāpiti Coast lies to the north, and the Remutaka Range divides the city from the plains of the Wairarapa. It lies at 41° 17' South and has a temperate maritime climate, generally windy all year with high rainfall.

In Māori oral history the explorer Kupe stayed in the harbour from about 925, and a later explorer, Whatonga, named it Te Whanganui-a-Tara after his son Tara. Iwi such as Rangitāne and Muaūpoko settled the area first; the disruptions of the Musket Wars in the early 19th century left them overwhelmed by northern iwi such as Te Āti Awa, who centred themselves at Pipitea.

European settlement began in 1839, when Colonel William Wakefield arrived to buy land for the New Zealand Company to sell to British settlers. In 1840 Captain William Mein Smith, the company's first Surveyor General, designed the town as interconnected grids that in practice spread along valleys and lower hill slopes. The settlers named it in November 1840, on the directors' suggestion, after Arthur Wellesley, the first Duke of Wellington, in recognition of his support for the company's principles of colonisation.

Earthquakes in 1848 destroyed most brick buildings, which led to the widespread use of timber. The Wairarapa earthquake of 1855, of an estimated magnitude of at least 8.2, raised land out of the harbour; much of it was later reclaimed and is now part of the central business district. The capital moved to Wellington in 1865, a status established by convention rather than in legislation.

Wellington is the capital of New Zealand and its third-largest city, with 210,800 people in the city and a metropolitan area including Lower Hutt, Porirua and Upper Hutt. The government, Parliament and Supreme Court are based there. Its architecture includes the Old Government Buildings, one of the largest wooden buildings in the world, and the Beehive, the executive wing of Parliament Buildings. It is the home of the National Archives, the National Library and the national museum, Te Papa, and is one of the country's chief seaports.
west-africa: West Africa is the westernmost region of Africa. Its climate is shaped by the dry Sahara to the north and east, which produces the Harmattan winds, and by the Atlantic Ocean to the south and west, which brings seasonal monsoons, so that biomes range from tropical forest to dry land. The Sahel, a transition zone between the Sudanian savannas and the Sahara, crosses several of its countries. The United Nations defines the region as 16 countries, from Mauritania and Senegal to Nigeria, with an area of about 6.1 million square kilometres.

West African hunter-gatherers occupied the coast by 12,000 years ago and moved north as far as Mali, Burkina Faso and Mauritania between 12,000 and 8000 years ago. Centralised states followed, beginning with Dhar Tichitt from 1600 BCE and Djenné-Djenno from 300 BCE. The Ghana Empire flourished roughly between the 2nd and 12th centuries CE and gave way to the Mali Empire. Positioned at a crossroads of trade between North Africa and the Sahel, the region supplied gold, ivory and advanced ironworking.

Portuguese traders began establishing settlements along the coast in 1445, followed by the French, English, Spanish, Danish and Dutch, and the African slave trade began not long after. It encouraged the formation of states such as the Bono state, the Bambara Empire and Dahomey, which exchanged slaves for European firearms. In the early 19th century Fulani reformist jihads swept across the region, among them Usman dan Fodio's Fulani Empire, which replaced the Hausa city-states. Britain and France then controlled nearly the whole region. Ghana under Kwame Nkrumah became the first West African colony to gain independence, in 1957, and by 1974 the region's nations were entirely autonomous.

The region is culturally and demographically diverse, home to the Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, Fulani, Akan, Mandé, Wolof, Songhai, Kanuri, Zarma, Tuareg and many other peoples. Islam, Christianity and traditional African religions are the most common religions. Its traditional building styles include the Sudano-Sahelian style in the inland areas and coastal forest styles, and typical formal dress includes the boubou robe and the Akan kente cloth.
west-bank: The West Bank is a landlocked territory on the western bank of the Jordan River, in the Levant. It is bordered by Jordan and the Dead Sea to the east and by Israel along the Green Line to the south, west and north. It has a land area of about 5,640 square kilometres and mostly rugged upland. Its elevation runs from the shore of the Dead Sea, 408 metres below sea level, to Mount Nabi Yunis at 1,030 metres. The name West Bank emerged for the territory occupied in 1948 and annexed in 1950 by Jordan, to distinguish it from Jordanian land east of the river.

From 1517 to 1917 the area was under Ottoman rule, as part of Ottoman Syria. In the early Ottoman period much of the northern West Bank formed part of the Turabay Emirate, a semi-autonomous Bedouin polity centred at Lajjun. Turkey renounced its claims in 1923, and the area became part of the British Mandate for Palestine. In 1947 the UN General Assembly recommended that it become part of a future Arab state, a proposal the Arab states opposed.

In the 1948 war the 1949 Armistice Agreements fixed the interim boundary between Israel and Jordan. After the Jericho Conference of December 1948, Transjordan annexed the area west of the river in 1950. Palestinian Arabs there were granted Jordanian citizenship and half the seats in the Jordanian parliament, and only the United Kingdom and Iraq recognised the annexation formally.

In June 1967 Israel captured the West Bank and East Jerusalem in the Six-Day War. Apart from East Jerusalem, the territory was not annexed, and it remained under military control until 1982. The Arab League summit at Rabat in 1974 named the Palestine Liberation Organization the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people. Jordan did not formally relinquish its claim until 1988. The Oslo Accords of 1993 left the final status of the territory to later negotiation.
west-bengal: West Bengal is on the eastern bottleneck of India, stretching from the Himalayas in the north to the Bay of Bengal in the south. The Darjeeling Himalayan hill region in the far north is part of the eastern Himalayas. The narrow Terai separates the hills from the plains of North Bengal, which give way southward to the Ganges delta, and the Sundarbans mangrove forests, part of the world's largest mangrove forest, mark the delta's southern edge.

Stone Age tools some 20,000 years old have been found in the state. According to the Mahabharata the region was part of the Vanga kingdom. Greek writers around 100 BCE mention a land called Gangaridai at the mouths of the Ganges. The region belonged to several pan-Indian empires, including those of the Mauryans and the Guptas, and the citadel of Gauḍa was the capital of the Gauda kingdom, the Pala Empire and the Sena Empire. After the Ghurid conquests led by Bakhtiyar Khalji, Islam spread across Bengal. Under the Bengal Sultanate the region was a major trading land, and it was absorbed into the Mughal Empire in 1576.

The British East India Company defeated the last independent Nawab, Siraj ud-Daulah, at the Battle of Plassey in 1757, and after the Battle of Buxar in 1764 it won the right to collect revenue in Bengal. The Bengal famine of 1770 claimed millions of lives. Calcutta, the company's headquarters, became the capital of British-held India, and from 1912 to 1947 it was the capital of the Bengal Province. The region was a centre of the Indian independence movement and of the Bengali Renaissance.

In 1947 the Bengal Legislative Council and Assembly voted to partition Bengal along religious lines. The western part, with a Hindu majority, became the Indian state of West Bengal; the eastern part went to Pakistan as East Bengal, later East Pakistan, and became Bangladesh in 1971. Refugees from the east arrived in large numbers for decades.

West Bengal is a state of India with Kolkata as its capital and largest city. Its population was 91,347,736 at the 2011 census. Bengali and English are the official languages, and the main ethnic group is the Bengalis. Its cultural heritage includes the Charyapada, Baul music, the songs of Rabindranath Tagore and the Bengal School of Art, and the state has three World Heritage sites.
west-germany: At the Yalta Conference of 4 to 11 February 1945, leaders of the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union agreed that post-war Germany would be divided into four occupation zones: French in the far west, British in the north-west, American in the south and Soviet in the east. Berlin was divided into four zones as well. The divisions were not meant to dismember Germany. The Federal Republic was founded on 23 May 1949 from twelve states formed in the three western zones, and at first it claimed an exclusive mandate for all of Germany. Three south-western states merged to form Baden-Württemberg in 1952, and the Saarland joined in 1957.

The Federal Republic obtained the full authority of a sovereign state on 5 May 1955 under the Bonn–Paris conventions, although full sovereignty came only with the Two Plus Four Agreement in 1990. It joined NATO on 9 May 1955. Konrad Adenauer was chancellor from 1949 to 1963, and he worked for full alignment with NATO and for agreements that grew into the European Union. Ludwig Erhard and Kurt Georg Kiesinger followed, and Willy Brandt became chancellor in October 1969. His Ostpolitik aimed to improve relations with Eastern Europe, and in 1970 he knelt at the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. Helmut Schmidt served from 1974 to 1982 and Helmut Kohl from 1982.

Denazification, an Allied programme to remove Nazi personnel and ideology from public life, was unpopular and opposed by Adenauer's government. Laws of 1951 granted amnesties and ended it, and many people with a Nazi past returned to the state apparatus. In 1967 the student Benno Ohnesorg was shot by a policeman during protests against emergency laws.

West Germany was a federal parliamentary republic with its capital at Bonn. The president was a largely ceremonial head of state, and the chancellor, elected by the Bundestag, headed the government. The upper house, the Bundesrat, represented the Länder. West Berlin was treated as an unofficial eleventh state, though it was under Allied control. After the opening of the Berlin Wall, East Germany voted to accede to the Federal Republic, and the five reconstituted eastern Länder and a reunited Berlin joined on 3 October 1990, raising the number of states from ten to sixteen. The reunited Germany is the direct continuation of West Germany and kept its memberships in NATO and the European Economic Community.
western-sahara: Western Sahara lies on the north-west coast of Africa, on the cusp of North Africa and West Africa, bordering the North Atlantic Ocean, Morocco, Algeria and Mauritania. It covers 272,000 square kilometres, mostly desert flatland. The coast is low and flat, and in the north the land rises to small mountains of up to 600 metres on the eastern side. There are no permanent streams, though spring flash floods occur, and a cool offshore current can bring fog and heavy dew. Summer highs in the interior reach 43 to 45 degrees.

The earliest known inhabitants were the Gaetuli. Roman-era sources describe the area as inhabited, depending on the century, by the Gaetulian Autololes or the Gaetulian Daradae. Other early inhabitants may have been the Bafour and the Serer; the Bafour were later replaced or absorbed by Berber-speaking populations, and religious and ethnic persecution of the Serer led to their southward migration in the 11th century. Islam arrived in the 8th century, and the territory may have been on caravan routes between Marrakesh and Tombouctou.

In the 11th century the Maqil Arabs settled in Morocco. Towards the end of the Almohad Caliphate the Beni Hassan, a sub-tribe of the Maqil, were called to put down a rebellion in the Sous. Under the Marinid dynasty they rebelled, were defeated by the Sultan and escaped beyond the dry river Saguia el-Hamra, where they were in constant war with the Lamtuna Berbers of the Sahara. Over roughly five centuries some Berber tribes mixed with the Maqil Arab tribes, forming a culture unique to Morocco and Mauritania.

Spanish colonisation lasted roughly from 1884 to 1976, and Spanish became one of the territory's main languages. Spain tried to transfer its administration to Morocco and Mauritania, though an advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice held that those countries had no sovereignty over Western Sahara. A war followed in which the Polisario Front proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic. Mauritania withdrew its claims in 1979 and Morocco secured control of most of the territory. A UN-sponsored ceasefire was reached in 1991.

The United Nations designates Western Sahara a non-self-governing territory, and sovereignty remains contested between Morocco and the Polisario Front, whose government in exile is based at Tindouf, Algeria. A wall about 2,700 kilometres long, the Berm, divides the territory. The main ethnic group is the Sahrawis, a mainly nomadic people of mixed Arab-Berber descent who speak the Hassānīya dialect of Arabic; they are Sunni Muslims of the Maliki school. Many were settled in refugee camps at Tindouf after 1975.
wiesbaden: Wiesbaden lies on the right bank of the Rhine above its confluence with the Main, at the southern foot of the Taunus mountains and opposite Mainz. The city centre is in the wide valley of the small Salzbach stream, and the city lies in the Rheingau wine-growing region. Frankfurt am Main is about 38 kilometres to the east. The site is a mountain basin protected by hills to the north and west, which gives it a mild climate. Three boroughs, Amöneburg, Kastel and Kostheim, were part of Mainz until 1945 and still carry Mainz in their names.

The first Roman fort, erected in 6 CE, housed an auxiliary cavalry unit, and the thermal springs are first mentioned by Pliny the Elder, who records them as noted for their pools for the horses of the Roman army. After the Franks defeated the Alamanni, they displaced them in this area during the sixth century, and in the eighth century Wiesbaden became the site of a royal palace of the Frankish kingdom. Einhard, the biographer of Charlemagne, first uses the name, as Wisabada, between 828 and 830.

From 1170 to 1629 the town lay in the County of Nassau, then in Nassau-Idstein until 1721, and in 1728 in the principality of Nassau-Usingen, whose house made Biebrich Palace its main residence in 1744. For its part in the German Peasants' War of 1525 Wiesbaden lost all its privileges for over forty years, and it became Protestant with the appointment of its first Lutheran pastor on 1 January 1543. The privileges were restored in 1566. In 1806 it became the capital of the Duchy of Nassau, and the ducal palace on the Schloßplatz was completed in November 1841.

After the First World War the city was occupied by the French army in 1918, and in 1921 the Wiesbaden Agreement on German reparations to France was signed there. After the Second World War, Wiesbaden suffered much less from bombing than Frankfurt and became the capital of the new state of Hesse.

Wiesbaden is the capital of Hesse and the state's second-largest city after Frankfurt. It is one of the oldest spa towns in Europe: its name means meadow baths, and fifteen mineral springs rise in the city centre, fourteen of them hot. By 1370 sixteen bath houses were in operation. The Neo-Classical Kurhaus, built between 1904 and 1907 at the request of Kaiser Wilhelm II, houses a casino. Other sights include the Russian Orthodox Church of Saint Elizabeth on the Neroberg, built from 1847 to 1855, and the Waterloo Obelisk on the Luisenplatz.
wilhelm-ii: Wilhelm was born on 27 January 1859 at the Crown Prince's Palace in Berlin, the son of Prince Frederick William of Prussia and Victoria, Princess Royal, the eldest child of Queen Victoria. He was the eldest of Victoria's 42 grandchildren. After 1871 he was second in line to the imperial throne, which under the constitution was held by the Prussian king.

His birth was traumatic, since the infant was in the breech position. His father succeeded as Frederick III after the death of Wilhelm I on 9 March 1888, but was already suffering from incurable throat cancer and died after 99 days, and on 15 June 1888 the 29-year-old Wilhelm became German Emperor and King of Prussia.

Bismarck's successor as chancellor, Leo von Caprivi, was followed by Chlodwig von Hohenlohe-Schillingsfürst in 1894 and by Bernhard von Bülow in 1900, whom Wilhelm regarded as his own Bismarck. Wilhelm promoted the arts and sciences and sponsored the Kaiser Wilhelm Society for scientific research. His impatient, impulsive handling of foreign policy brought a series of incidents: the Kruger telegram of 1896, his speech of 1900 telling German soldiers leaving for China to be merciless in the spirit of the Huns, and a visit to Tangier on 31 March 1905 that set off the Moroccan Crisis.
The Daily Telegraph Affair of 1908 damaged him badly, and he had less influence for the rest of his reign. A naval programme under Alfred von Tirpitz, from 1897, set Germany against Britain.

In the war he was a shadow Kaiser, confined to ceremonial duties; by 1916 the empire was effectively a military dictatorship under Hindenburg and Ludendorff. He could not decide whether to abdicate in the revolution of 1918, hoping to keep the Prussian crown, but the imperial crown was tied to it.

Wilhelm went into exile in the Netherlands and lived at Doorn. In 1922 he published the first volume of his memoirs, insisting that he was not guilty of starting the war. His first wife, Augusta Victoria, died on 11 April 1921, and on 5 November 1922 he married Hermine Reuss of Greiz. He died of a pulmonary embolism at Doorn on 4 June 1941, aged 82.

Hitler wanted a state funeral in Berlin, but Wilhelm had ordered that his body not return to Germany unless the monarchy was restored. Writing about him has followed three trends: court writers who saw a martyr, those who judged him unable to bear his responsibilities, and, after 1950, scholars seeking an objective portrait.
william-blake: William Blake was born on 28 November 1757 in Soho, London, the third of seven children of James Blake, a hosier, and Catherine Blake. He attended school only long enough to learn to read and write and was otherwise educated at home by his mother. The family were Moravians and English Dissenters. The Bible was a profound influence on him throughout his life,.

On 4 August 1772 he was apprenticed to the engraver James Basire for seven years and then became a professional engraver. In 1779 he entered the Royal Academy, where he came to detest the ideas of its first president, Joshua Reynolds, who prized general truth and general beauty. Blake wrote in the margin of Reynolds's Discourses that to generalise is to be an idiot. In 1782 he married Catherine Boucher, who became his partner in work as printer and colourist.

About 1783 patronage allowed him to publish his first poems, Poetical Sketches. In 1784 he opened a print shop with James Parker and began to work with the radical publisher Joseph Johnson, whose circle included Joseph Priestley, Mary Wollstonecraft and Thomas Paine. Blake had great hopes for the French and American revolutions but despaired at the Reign of Terror.

In 1788 he invented relief etching, or illuminated printing, with which he produced most of his later books. He drew words and images backwards in acid-resistant varnish on copper plates and let acid bite away the rest, so that the design stood in relief. His commercial work consisted largely of intaglio engraving. In 1800 he moved to Felpham in Sussex to illustrate the works of William Hayley, and began Milton there. He returned to London in 1804 and began Jerusalem.

Blake lived in London all his life except for three years at Felpham, and was considered mad by contemporaries for his idiosyncratic views. He was hostile to the Church of England and to almost all organised religion, and was influenced by Emanuel Swedenborg. His early work, such as The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, is rebellious and protests against dogmatic religion. In the later Milton and Jerusalem he presents a humanity redeemed by self-sacrifice and forgiveness. The preface to Milton includes the poem beginning And did those feet in ancient time, which became the words of the anthem Jerusalem.
Blake died on 12 August 1827 at Fountain Court, off the Strand, having worked on his Dante series that day. Largely unrecognised during his life, he became a seminal figure of the Romantic age,.
william-henry-harrison: William Henry Harrison was born on 9 February 1773 at Berkeley Plantation on the James River in Virginia, the youngest of seven children of Benjamin Harrison V, who signed the Declaration of Independence and served as governor of Virginia. He was the last United States president born a British subject. On 16 August 1791, aged 18, he was commissioned an ensign in the United States Army and assigned to Fort Washington at Cincinnati during the Northwest Indian War. He married Anna Tuthill Symmes on 25 November 1795, after eloping when her father refused permission.

Harrison was appointed secretary of the Northwest Territory in 1798 and elected its delegate to Congress in 1799, where he championed settlers who wanted lower land prices. As governor of Indiana Territory from 10 January 1801 he made his home at Vincennes, built Grouseland there in 1805 and founded a university that was incorporated as Vincennes University in 1806. His treaties with American Indian leaders ceded large tracts of land to the nation. Resistance to expansion grew under Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa. After the War of 1812 he sat in the House of Representatives from 1816 to 1819 and was elected to the Senate in 1824. He lost the presidential race of 1836 as one of four Whig candidates and won in 1840.

Harrison took the oath of office on 4 March 1841, a cold, wet day, without a hat or overcoat, and delivered the longest inaugural address in American history, at 8,445 words. His brief term was marked by a struggle with Henry Clay over patronage. After a walk in the rain on 24 March he fell ill, and his doctors diagnosed pneumonia. John Tyler was sworn in on 6 April. His death exposed an ambiguity in Article II of the Constitution about whether the vice president became president or only assumed the duties of the office. Congress voted his widow Anna a pension of $25,000.
william-howard-taft: William Howard Taft was born on 15 September 1857 in Cincinnati, Ohio, to Alphonso Taft and Louise Torrey. His father served as a judge and an ambassador, and was United States Secretary of War and Attorney General under President Ulysses S. Grant. Taft attended Yale University and the Cincinnati Law School. After admission to the Ohio bar he was appointed assistant prosecutor for Hamilton County in October 1880 and Collector of Internal Revenue for Ohio's First District by President Chester A. Arthur in 1882. His professional goal was always a seat on the Supreme Court.

In 1890 Harrison appointed Taft Solicitor General, and from 1892 to 1900 he served as a federal judge of the Sixth Circuit. In 1900 President William McKinley asked him to join the commission to organise a civilian government in the Philippines, with the assurance of the next Supreme Court vacancy. Taft accepted on condition that he head the commission, and sailed in April 1900. In 1902 he refused a Supreme Court seat from Theodore Roosevelt because his work in the islands was not done. He became Secretary of War in 1904, and Roosevelt made him his chosen successor.

Taft defeated William Jennings Bryan in 1908 and was sworn in on 4 March 1909. As president he focused on East Asia more than Europe and repeatedly intervened to prop up or remove Latin American governments. He restructured the State Department, which was for the first time organised into geographical divisions. He brought 70 antitrust suits in four years, against Roosevelt's 40 in seven, and made six appointments to the Supreme Court. Disputes over the tariff, conservation and antitrust cases separated him from Roosevelt, who challenged him for the Republican nomination in 1912. Taft kept a bare majority of delegates and Roosevelt left the party. In the three-way election Taft carried only Utah and Vermont, and Woodrow Wilson won.

He returned to Yale as a professor and worked against war through the League to Enforce Peace. In 1921 President Warren G. Harding appointed him chief justice. On the court he was conservative on business issues, individual rights advanced under him, and his work on administrative reform culminated in the Judiciary Act of 1925.

In poor health, Taft resigned in February 1930 and died on 8 March 1930. He was the first president and the first Supreme Court justice buried at Arlington National Cemetery. He is the only person to have been both president and chief justice.
william-mckinley: William McKinley Jr. was born in 1843 in Niles, Ohio, the seventh of nine children of William McKinley Sr. and Nancy Allison McKinley. When the Civil War began in 1861 he and his cousin William McKinley Osbourne enlisted as privates in the Poland Guards, which became part of the 23rd Ohio Infantry. He received a commission as second lieutenant in recognition of his service at Antietam and ended the war as a brevet major, the only president to begin as an enlisted man and finish at that rank.
After the war he studied law and was admitted to the bar in Warren, Ohio, in March 1867. That year he moved to Canton, Ohio, where he practised law and later married Ida Saxton.

McKinley was elected to Congress in 1876 and became the Republican expert on the protective tariff. Democrats repeatedly redistricted his seat to remove him; he won anyway in 1878 and 1884. His McKinley Tariff of 1890 was highly controversial and, with another Democratic redistricting, contributed to his defeat that year. He was elected governor of Ohio in 1891 and 1893.

In 1896, amid a deep depression, he won the Republican nomination with the help of Mark Hanna and defeated the Democrat William Jennings Bryan in a front-porch campaign. He backed the gold standard unless altered by international agreement and promised that high tariffs would restore prosperity. In office he signed the Dingley Tariff of 1897 and the Gold Standard Act of 1900.

The United States annexed Hawaii in 1898. McKinley hoped to persuade Spain to grant Cuba independence without conflict, but when talks failed he requested and signed Congress's declaration of war in the Spanish–American War of 1898. Spain turned over Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, and Cuba was promised independence but stayed under American control until 1902. A pro-independence rebellion began in the Philippines and was eventually suppressed.

McKinley defeated Bryan again in 1900. On 6 September 1901 the anarchist Leon Czolgosz shot him, and he died eight days later. Vice President Theodore Roosevelt succeeded him, and Roosevelt's popularity overshadowed McKinley's legacy. Historians regard the election of 1896 as a realignment that began the Republican-dominated Fourth Party System.
william-shakespeare: William Shakespeare was the son of John Shakespeare, an alderman and glove-maker originally from Snitterfield in Warwickshire, and Mary Arden, whose affluent landowning family was influential in the Recusant Catholic community. He was baptised in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564. His date of birth is unknown, but it is traditionally observed on 23 April, which is also the day he died in 1616. He was the third of eight children. Most biographers agree he was probably educated at the King's New School in Stratford, although no attendance records survive.

At 18 he married 26-year-old Anne Hathaway, and a marriage licence was issued on 27 November 1582. Their daughter Susanna was baptised on 26 May 1583, and the twins Hamnet and Judith on 2 February 1585. Hamnet died at the age of 11 and was buried on 11 August 1596. Sometime between 1585 and 1592 Shakespeare began a career in London as an actor, writer and part-owner of the Lord Chamberlain's Men.

Shakespeare produced most of his known works between 1589 and 1613. His first recorded works are Richard III and the three parts of Henry VI, written in the early 1590s, and his first histories draw heavily on the 1587 edition of Raphael Holinshed's Chronicles. When the theatres were closed by plague in 1593 and 1594, he published the narrative poems Venus and Adonis and The Rape of Lucrece, dedicated to Henry Wriothesley, 3rd Earl of Southampton. The 154 Sonnets were printed in 1609, though evidence suggests he wrote sonnets throughout his career for a private readership.

His verse is mostly blank verse in iambic pentameter. His early plays follow the conventional, rhetorical style of the day, and by the mid-1590s, in Romeo and Juliet, Richard II and A Midsummer Night's Dream, he had begun to write a more natural poetry. He used soliloquies to explore characters' minds, and he wrote mainly tragedies until 1608, then tragicomedies such as The Winter's Tale and The Tempest.

At about 49, around 1613, Shakespeare appears to have retired to Stratford, where he died three years later. Few records of his private life survive. In 1623 two fellow actors, John Heminges and Henry Condell, published the First Folio, which includes 36 of his plays, with a poem by Ben Jonson calling him 'not of an age, but for all time'.

Doubts about authorship first appeared some 230 years after his death, naming candidates such as Francis Bacon, Christopher Marlowe and Edward de Vere, 17th Earl of Oxford, but all but a few scholars regard this as a fringe theory. Samuel Johnson quoted him more often than any other author in his Dictionary.
william-wordsworth: William Wordsworth was born on 7 April 1770 at Cockermouth, Cumberland, the second of five children of John Wordsworth and Ann Cookson. His sister, the poet and diarist Dorothy Wordsworth, to whom he remained close, was born the following year. His mother died in 1778 and his father in 1783, and his father had set him to memorise long passages of Milton, Shakespeare and Spenser. He attended Hawkshead Grammar School and took his BA at St John's College, Cambridge, in 1791.

In November 1791 he visited Revolutionary France and fell in love with Annette Vallon, who in 1792 gave birth to their daughter Caroline. Financial problems and tense relations between Britain and France forced him back to England alone the following year, and the Reign of Terror left him disillusioned.

A legacy of £900 from Raisley Calvert in 1795 allowed him to pursue poetry, and that year he met Samuel Taylor Coleridge in Somerset. In 1797 he and Dorothy moved to Alfoxton House, a few miles from Coleridge's home. Together the two poets, with insights from Dorothy, produced Lyrical Ballads in 1798, which included Wordsworth's Tintern Abbey and Coleridge's The Rime of the Ancient Mariner. The second edition of 1800 named only Wordsworth and carried the preface in which some scholars see a central work of Romantic literary theory.

In the winter of 1798-99 at Goslar he began the autobiographical poem later titled The Prelude. In 1799 he and Dorothy settled at Dove Cottage in Grasmere, and Wordsworth, Coleridge and Robert Southey came to be known as the Lake Poets. On 4 October 1802 he married Mary Hutchinson, a childhood friend, after visiting Annette and Caroline in Calais with Dorothy.

He completed the first version of The Prelude in 1805 but would not publish so personal a work before finishing The Recluse. Poems, in Two Volumes appeared in 1807 and included the Ode: Intimations of Immortality, but its reception was lukewarm. In 1813 he became Distributor of Stamps for Westmorland, a post that made him financially secure, and the family moved to Rydal Mount, where he spent the rest of his life. The Excursion, published in 1814, was the second part of The Recluse, whose other parts he never completed. He was Poet Laureate from 1843 until his death from pleurisy on 23 April 1850.
willy-brandt: Willy Brandt was born Herbert Ernst Karl Frahm in the Free City of Lübeck on 18 December 1913. His mother was a single parent who worked as a department store cashier, and he never met his father. He joined the Socialist Youth in 1929 and in 1930, at sixteen, became a full member of the Social Democratic Party. He also wrote for the Volksbote, a local Social Democrat daily, under its editor Julius Leber. In exile he took the name Willy Brandt as a pseudonym to avoid detection by Nazi agents, formally adopting it in 1948.

Brandt was elected to the Bundestag in 1949 from West Berlin. From October 1957 to 1966 he was Governing Mayor of West Berlin, a period of rising tension that led to the construction of the Berlin Wall. He then served as foreign minister and vice chancellor in Kurt Georg Kiesinger's cabinet. After the 1969 elections the SPD and the Free Democratic Party formed a coalition and the Bundestag elected Brandt chancellor.

His Ostpolitik developed by stages: in 1967 he established diplomatic relations with Romania, and in 1968 he restored them with Yugoslavia. He met the East German premier Willi Stoph at Erfurt on 19 March 1970 and at Kassel on 21 May 1970. Ostpolitik cost the coalition its narrow majority, and in 1972 new elections were called, in which he led the SPD to its best-ever federal result. Günter Guillaume, one of his personal assistants, was arrested on 24 April 1974 and later sentenced to 13 years for treason. Brandt resigned on 6 May 1974, though he stayed in the Bundestag and as party chairman until 1987.

From 1976 to 1992 Brandt was president of the Socialist International, and in 1977 he became chairman of the Independent Commission for International Developmental Issues, whose report of 1980 became known as the Brandt Report. In late 1989 he was among the first left-wing leaders in West Germany to favour quick reunification. He died of colon cancer at his home in Unkel on 8 October 1992, aged 78, and was given a state funeral. The SPD's headquarters in Berlin is named the Willy Brandt Haus, and a memorial to him and the kneeling at Warsaw was unveiled in Warsaw in 2000.
windhoek: Windhoek lies in central Namibia on the Khomas Highland plateau, at about 1,700 m above sea level, in the geographical centre of the country. The city grew up around a hot spring known to the pastoral peoples of the area, and twelve strong springs later supplied water for gardens and grain. Rocky, mountainous ground to the south, east and west makes building costly, which leaves the area to the north as the main direction for expansion.

In 1840 Jonker Afrikaner, captain of the Orlam, settled near one of the main springs in what is now the suburb of Klein Windhoek. He built a stone church that held 500 people and also served as a school. The Rhenish missionaries Carl Hugo Hahn and Franz Heinrich Kleinschmidt began work there in late 1842 but two years later were driven out by the Methodist Wesleyans Richard Haddy and Joseph Tindall. A series of wars between the Nama and the Herero destroyed the settlement, and in June 1885 a Swiss botanist found only jackals and starving guinea fowl among the neglected fruit trees.

Germany declared a protectorate over what became German South West Africa in 1884. Major Curt von François, commanding the Schutztruppe, placed his garrison at Windhoek as a buffer between the Nama and the Herero, and on 18 October 1890 he fixed the foundation stone of the fort now called the Alte Feste. Growth accelerated after 1907 as people came from the countryside to find work. South Africa occupied the territory in 1915, and from 1920 administered it under a League of Nations mandate. In 1971 a strike of contract workers, aimed at ending the contract labour system, began in Windhoek.

Windhoek has been the national capital since independence in 1990 and is also the capital of the Khomas Region. Its population was 486,186 in 2023. The University of Namibia, the national theatre, the National Museum in the Alte Feste and the Independence Memorial Museum stand there. The Tintenpalast, built in 1912 and 1913, houses the Parliament. The Reiterdenkmal, which commemorated the German victory over the Herero and Nama in the genocide of 1904 to 1907, was moved in December 2013 from its place beside the Christuskirche to the yard of the Alte Feste.
winston-churchill: Winston Leonard Spencer Churchill was born on 30 November 1874 at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire. On his father's side he was a descendant of John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough. His father, Lord Randolph Churchill, was a Conservative MP, and his mother, Jennie, was the daughter of the American businessman Leonard Jerome. He joined the British Army in 1895 and saw action in British India, the Mahdist War and the Second Boer War, gaining fame as a war correspondent.

Elected a Conservative MP in 1900, Churchill defected to the Liberals in 1904. In 1908 H. H. Asquith made him President of the Board of Trade, and at 33 he was the youngest Cabinet member since 1866. After the failed naval attack on the Dardanelles he resigned from the government on 25 November 1915 and served on the Western Front, commanding the 6th Royal Scots Fusiliers from January 1916. Under David Lloyd George he returned as Minister of Munitions in 1917. As Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1924 he restored the gold standard in April 1925, against the advice of economists including John Maynard Keynes; the return is held to have caused deflation and unemployment.

During the 1930s he was out of government, in his "wilderness years". He was reappointed First Lord of the Admiralty on 3 September 1939 and became prime minister in May 1940, succeeding Neville Chamberlain. He formed a war cabinet that included the Labour leader Clement Attlee. In 1946, as Leader of the Opposition, he gave his "Iron Curtain" speech in America.

Churchill wrote prolifically, including the six-volume The Second World War and A History of the English-Speaking Peoples, and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953. He also painted hundreds of works. He resigned on 5 April 1955 and remained an MP until 1964. Elizabeth II offered to make him Duke of London, but he declined. He died on 24 January 1965 and was given a state funeral. He is generally viewed as a victorious wartime leader, though as a staunch imperialist he has sometimes been criticised for comments on race and for wartime decisions such as area bombing.
wisconsin: Wisconsin lies between the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River and is divided into five regions. The Lake Superior Lowland runs along the north shore, and the Northern Highland has mixed forests, thousands of glacial lakes and the state's highest point, Timms Hill. The Central Plain has the sandstone formations of the Dells of the Wisconsin River and rich farmland. The Eastern Ridges and Lowlands in the southeast hold many of the largest cities, and the Western Upland, part of the Driftless Area, is a rugged landscape of bluffs along the Mississippi. Forest covers 46 per cent of the land.

The first people arrived around 10,000 BCE, during the Wisconsin Glaciation. These Paleo-Indians hunted ice age animals such as the Boaz mastodon, whose skeleton was found with spear points in the south-west. After the ice age ended around 8000 BCE, the Archaic peoples lived by hunting, fishing and gathering. Agricultural societies emerged over the Woodland period, from 1000 BCE to 1000 CE, and towards its end Wisconsin was the heartland of the Effigy Mound culture, which built thousands of animal-shaped mounds. Between 1000 and 1500 CE the Mississippian and Oneota cultures built substantial settlements, including the fortified village at Aztalan.

At European contact the Menominee, Ho-Chunk and Iowa shared the region. The Ojibwe, Sauk, Meskwaki, Kickapoo and Potawatomi had migrated there from the east between 1500 and 1700. The French explorer Jacques Marquette was the first European to reach the Wisconsin River, in 1673, which he called Meskousing. The French later wrote Ouisconsin, and English speakers anglicised it as they arrived in large numbers in the early 19th century. The legislature of Wisconsin Territory made the present spelling official in 1845. The meaning is obscure, though a leading theory takes it from the Miami word Meskonsing, meaning it lies red, after the reddish sandstone of the Dells.

Wisconsin was originally part of the Northwest Territory and was admitted as a state in 1848. Miners, many of them Cornish, settled the south-west, and the nickname Badger State comes from miners who burrowed into hillsides. They were followed by migrants from New England and upstate New York, who dominated heavy industry, finance, politics and education in the early years of statehood. Between 1850 and 1900 most immigrants were Germans, Scandinavians, Irish and Poles. The Republican Party was founded in Wisconsin in 1854.

Madison is the capital and Milwaukee the most populous city. The state is divided into 72 counties and is home to eleven federally recognised tribes. It remains a centre of German American and Scandinavian American culture, and it is known as America's Dairyland, particularly for its cheese. Taliesin and the Jacobs I House, designed by the Wisconsin-born architect Frank Lloyd Wright, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wolfgang-amadeus-mozart: Mozart was born on 27 January 1756 at Getreidegasse 9 in Salzburg, the capital of the Archbishopric of Salzburg, an ecclesiastical principality within the Holy Roman Empire. He was the youngest of seven children, five of whom died in infancy. His father, Leopold Mozart, a native of Augsburg, was a minor composer and an experienced teacher who became deputy Kapellmeister of the Salzburg orchestra in 1763. Mozart was trained on the harpsichord and also became skilled at violin, singing and dancing.

At five he was competent on keyboard and violin, had begun to compose and had performed before European royalty. His father took him on a grand tour of Europe and then three trips to Italy. A fruitless search for employment in 1777 to 1779 led through Paris, Mannheim and Munich and back to Salzburg. While visiting Vienna in 1781 his quarrels with his Salzburg employers came to a head and he was dismissed.

Mozart stayed in Vienna for the rest of his life, achieving fame and some financial success but no long-term security. His early Vienna years produced the opera Die Entführung aus dem Serail, the Great Mass in C minor and the Haydn Quartets. He composed more than a dozen piano concertos there. In 1783 he bought a fortepiano by Anton Walter, which he played often in the city's concerts, and which survives in Salzburg. He lived at the centre of the Viennese musical world and knew Joseph Haydn and some of the court of Emperor Joseph II.

In his final years he wrote the last three symphonies, ending with the Jupiter, the serenade Eine kleine Nachtmusik, the Clarinet Concerto, and the operas Le nozze di Figaro, Don Giovanni, Così fan tutte and Die Zauberflöte. Biographers rely on about 1500 pages of family letters, early biographies and surviving manuscripts, and they judge the publisher Friedrich Rochlitz untrustworthy, since he published false stories to increase sales.

Mozart died on 5 December 1791 at the age of 35, leaving the Requiem largely unfinished. Publishers soon sought a complete edition of his works. Breitkopf & Härtel and Johann Anton André negotiated with his widow Constanze, and the publication helped rescue her and her two children from poverty. Ludwig Ritter von Köchel completed the first catalogue in 1862, and his numbers, marked K or KV, remain the standard way to identify a work.

His music with Haydn's stands as an archetype of the Classical style, with clarity, balance and transparency as its hallmarks. He almost single-handedly developed the Classical piano concerto. Ludwig van Beethoven, fifteen years his junior, was deeply influenced by his work. Salzburg, which he left in frustration in 1781, has two museums in his former homes, the Salzburg Festival and the International Mozarteum Foundation.
woodrow-wilson: Thomas Woodrow Wilson was born on 28 December 1856 in Staunton, Virginia, the son of Joseph Ruggles Wilson, a Presbyterian pastor, and Jessie Janet Woodrow. Before he was two the family moved to Augusta, Georgia. After a PhD in history and political science at Johns Hopkins University he taught at Bryn Mawr College from 1885 to 1888, where his 1887 article The Study of Administration argued that public administration should be a field of study of its own. In June 1902 the trustees of Princeton University made him its president. He raised admission standards, introduced academic departments and groups of students guided by preceptors, and worked to keep African Americans out of the school. He served as governor of New Jersey from 1911 to 1913.

In the 1912 election Wilson defeated President William Howard Taft and the former president Theodore Roosevelt, and became the first Southerner elected president since Zachary Taylor. In April 1913 he addressed Congress in person to set out his New Freedom programme. Its early measures included the Revenue Act of 1913, which began the modern income tax, and the Federal Reserve Act. His administration intervened often in Latin America, sending troops to occupy the Dominican Republic and intervene in Haiti, and in his first year he authorised the widespread imposition of racial segregation in the federal bureaucracy.

The United States declared neutrality when the First World War began in 1914, and Wilson was narrowly re-elected in 1916 on the slogan He Kept Us Out of War. After Germany began unrestricted submarine warfare in January 1917 and the Zimmermann Telegram became public, he asked Congress in April 1917 for a declaration of war. He issued the Fourteen Points, which the Allies and Germany accepted as a basis for peace. He led the American delegation to the Paris Peace Conference, the first incumbent president to travel to Europe, and secured the League of Nations as part of the Treaty of Versailles. At home he rejected a Republican compromise that would have let the Senate ratify the treaty and join the League.

Wilson had a stroke in October 1919 that left him incapacitated, and his wife and his physician controlled access to him. Republicans won the 1920 election in a landslide. He died in February 1924 at the age of 67. Historians have criticised him for supporting racial segregation, while crediting his administration with the Federal Reserve, the Federal Trade Commission and the graduated income tax, and regarding him as a key figure in the making of modern American liberalism.
world-health-organization: International cooperation on disease began with the International Sanitary Conferences, the first of which met in Paris on 23 June 1851 and which continued until 1938. The first was almost solely concerned with cholera. With the causes of epidemic diseases still disputed, agreement was hard to reach: seven conferences over 41 years were convened before any produced a multi-state agreement. The seventh, at Venice in 1892, finally resulted in a convention on the sanitary control of shipping through the Suez Canal, and in 1897 a convention on bubonic plague was signed by sixteen of the nineteen states attending.

The conferences led to the founding of the Pan-American Sanitary Bureau in 1902 and the Office International d'Hygiène Publique in 1907, and the League of Nations created its own Health Organization in 1920. After World War II, the United Nations assembled the health organizations to form the WHO. The World Health Organization was established on 7 April 1948 and began its work on 1 September 1948, taking over the assets and duties of the League's Health Organization and the Paris office, including the International Classification of Diseases.

The organisation is governed by the World Health Assembly, made up of its member states, which elects an executive board of 34 health specialists, selects the director-general and approves the budget. Its funds come mainly from member states, and then from private donors. The headquarters in Geneva was designed by the Swiss architect Jean Tschumi and inaugurated in 1966. Its regional divisions were created between 1949 and 1952, following the model of the Pan American Health Organization, and it has six regional offices and 150 country offices.

The organisation played a leading role in the eradication of smallpox, the near-eradication of polio and the development of an Ebola vaccine. It launched its Global Polio Eradication Initiative in 1988, working with Rotary International, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and UNICEF, and helped to reduce cases by 99%. In the 1970s it dropped its commitment to a global malaria eradication campaign as too ambitious. Since the late 20th century, new actors in global health such as the World Bank and the Gates Foundation have weakened its role as coordinator, and it also coordinated the international response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
world-trade-organization: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade was set up by a multilateral treaty of 23 countries after World War II, alongside other new institutions for economic cooperation such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. A proposed International Trade Organization never started, because the United States and other signatories did not ratify its treaty, so the GATT slowly became a de facto international organisation, operating for almost half a century as a provisional, semi-institutionalised treaty regime. Seven rounds of negotiation between 1949 and 1979 first cut tariffs. The Kennedy Round of the mid-sixties produced an anti-dumping agreement, and the Tokyo Round of the seventies made the first major attempt to tackle barriers that were not tariffs.

The eighth round, the Uruguay Round, was launched at Punta del Este in September 1986. It extended the system to services and intellectual property and reformed trade in agriculture and textiles. Its Final Act, the Marrakesh Agreement, was signed on 15 April 1994, and the WTO was established on 1 January 1995, with its headquarters in Geneva.

The WTO provides a framework for negotiating trade agreements and for settling disputes among its members. Its agreements cover goods, services and intellectual property, and rest on non-discrimination, expressed in the most-favoured-nation and national treatment provisions, with exceptions for purposes such as environmental protection and national security. Its highest body, the Ministerial Conference, usually meets every two years and decides by consensus. The General Council, made up of representatives of all members, handles day-to-day business, and a Secretariat led by a Director-General administers the organisation.

Unlike the GATT, whose rules were ambiguous and which let members block dispute settlement, the WTO has more numerous and more precise obligations, and members that do not comply may face punishment. Its consensus rule has also contributed to deadlock. Ministerial conferences have sometimes been contentious: the Seattle conference of 1999 provoked large demonstrations, and Doha in 2001 approved China's entry.

The Doha Development Round, launched in November 2001, aimed to make globalisation more inclusive and to cut barriers and subsidies in farming. Talks stalled over differences between developed nations and major low-income and lower-middle-income countries, and over agricultural subsidies in the European Union and the United States. The Hong Kong conference agreed to phase out agricultural export subsidies, and the Bali Ministerial Declaration of 2013 addressed bureaucratic barriers to commerce. Economic studies generally find that the WTO has boosted trade and reduced trade barriers. Critics argue that the benefits of free trade are not shared equally, that its agreements may disadvantage developing countries and that commercial interests have been put before environmental and labour concerns.
world-wide-web: Tim Berners-Lee was motivated by the problem of storing, updating and finding documents and data files in CERN, a large and constantly changing organisation, and of distributing them to collaborators outside it. In his design he rejected the tree structure used in the existing CERNDOC documentation system and in the Unix filesystem, as well as approaches that tagged files with keywords, as in the VAX/NOTES system. He adopted instead concepts he had put into practice in his private ENQUIRE system of 1980. Learning of Ted Nelson's hypertext model of 1965, in which documents are linked in unconstrained ways through hot spots embedded in the text, helped confirm that his concept was sound.

A competing system, Gopher, was created in 1991 around a hierarchical model of menus that held pointers to documents and to other menus, whereas a document on the Web holds both its content and its links. Gopher grew at first, with nearly seven thousand servers known by April 1994, but then declined while the Web accelerated. Its more rigid structure, bad early publicity and the decision not to follow open collaboration principles were among the reasons.

The Internet and the Web are not the same thing. The Internet is a global system of interconnected computer networks, while the Web is a collection of documents and other resources linked by hyperlinks and URLs and fetched with the Hypertext Transfer Protocol. The usual document is a web page written in Hypertext Markup Language, which supports text, images, audio, video and scripts as well as links. A browser requests a page from a web server, and in the 1990s following links from page to page came to be called browsing or web surfing.

The prefix www in many web addresses follows the old practice of naming a host after the service it provides, as ftp or news were. No standard requires it. According to Paolo Palazzi, who worked at CERN with Berners-Lee, its popular use was accidental: the project page was meant to sit at www.cern.ch, with info.cern.ch as CERN's home page, but the records were never switched, and others copied the practice. The first web server was nxoc01.cern.ch.

Links break as pages are moved or replaced, a phenomenon called link rot, and the Internet Archive, active since 1996, is the best known of many efforts to archive websites. Archie, an index of FTP files released in 1990, was the first search engine. In December 2007 Unicode passed ASCII and Western European encodings as the most used character map on the Web.
wroclaw: Wrocław lies on the banks of the Oder in the Silesian Lowlands, at an elevation of around 105 to 156 metres, and is supplied within the city limits by four tributaries: the Bystrzyca, Oława, Ślęza and Widawa. It is the capital of the Lower Silesian Voivodeship, created in 1999, and a major transport hub on routes between Western and Central Europe and the rest of Poland.

A place called Budorigum, at or near the site, appears on Claudius Ptolemy's map of 142 to 147 CE. The Ślężans, a West Slavic tribe, built a fortified gord on Ostrów Tumski. The city became part of the Piast-ruled Polish state in the late 10th century, and the Diocese of Wrocław was founded in 1000 under the Archbishopric of Gniezno. From the 13th century migration from German-speaking regions contributed to its growth, and German gradually became its predominant language. In the 14th century it passed to the Bohemian Crown.

The Reformation reached the city in 1518, but from 1526 Silesia was ruled by the Catholic House of Habsburg. During the Thirty Years' War the city lost thousands of inhabitants to plague. In 1811 the Viadrina university of Frankfurt an der Oder was moved to Breslau and united with the Jesuit university, forming what is now the University of Wrocław. It became part of the German Empire in 1871. In November 1939 the Germans imprisoned 173 Polish professors from Kraków's universities in the city before deporting them to Sachsenhausen. After 1945 it became part of Poland, and its German inhabitants who had not fled were expelled between 1945 and 1949.

Wrocław is the third-largest city of Poland and the historical capital of Silesia, with over 130,000 students. Its Market Square is one of the largest in Europe, and its Town Hall is the oldest preserved in Poland. The Centennial Hall is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Old Town, with Brick Gothic and Baroque buildings, is on Poland's list of national monuments. The Wrocław Zoo is the oldest in Poland, and the city has been the seat of a Catholic archdiocese since the diocese of 1000.
wuhan: Wuhan lies in east-central Hubei, on the eastern Jianghan Plain, where the Han River flows into the Yangtze. The two rivers divide the urban area into three districts, Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, known together as the Three Towns of Wuhan. The name joins Wu, for Wuchang, and Han, for Hankou, whose name means Mouth of the Han. The city has long been called the Nine Provinces' Thoroughfare, and its position has also exposed it to flooding.

The Wuhan area has been settled for about 3,500 years. Panlongcheng, an archaeological site associated mainly with the Erligang culture, lies in Huangpi District. In the Han dynasty Hanyang became a fairly busy port, and walls were built to protect Hanyang in 206 and Wuchang in 223, the latter marking the foundation of Wuhan. In 223 Sun Quan, leader of the Eastern Wu, ordered the Yellow Crane Tower built on the Wuchang side, one of the Four Great Towers of China.

On 10 October 1911 the Wuchang Uprising, launched by followers of Sun Yat-sen, led to the collapse of the Qing state, ending 2,000 years of dynastic rule. In 1927 the Kuomintang government moved its capital from Guangzhou to Wuhan and combined Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang into Wuhan City. Wuhan was briefly a capital again in 1937, as a provisional wartime capital, and in 1938, during the Second Sino-Japanese War, it was the site of the Battle of Wuhan. After 1949 the Communists rebuilt its war-damaged industry, and Wuhan Iron and Steel opened in 1958.

Wuhan is the capital of Hubei and the largest city in the province. It is a major transport hub and the centre of Central China, with institutions such as Wuhan University and the Huazhong University of Science and Technology.
wurzburg: Würzburg is the second-largest city in Franconia after Nuremberg and spans both banks of the Main river. A Bronze Age refuge castle, the Celtic Segodunum and later a Roman fort stood on the Leistenberg, where Fortress Marienberg now stands. Alamanni settled the area in the 4th or 5th century and Franks followed in the 6th and 7th. A Merovingian duke had his seat there from about 650, and Irish missionaries including Kilian Christianized it in 686. A donation of 1 May 704 mentions the place as Virteburch.

The bishops of Würzburg built a secular lordship that reached into Eastern Franconia in the 12th century, and the Prince-Bishopric of Würzburg is dated 1168 to 1803. The city hosted several Imperial Diets, including that of 1180, which banned Henry the Lion. Charlemagne consecrated a first church on the cathedral's site in 788, and the present Romanesque cathedral was built from 1040 to 1225. The University of Würzburg was founded in 1402 and re-founded in 1582 by Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn. In 1400 the bishop's troops defeated the citizens at the Battle of Bergtheim, and the city stayed under his control. Jews were massacred in 1147 and 1298.

In the Peasants' War, about 8,000 peasants were killed outside the city on 4 June 1525. The council member Tilman Riemenschneider refused to fight them and was imprisoned and tortured at Marienberg with the entire council. Between 1626 and 1631, under Bishop Philip Adolf, an estimated 600 to 900 alleged witches were burnt, until King Gustaf Adolf of Sweden invaded. The Residence was begun in 1720. The city passed to Bavaria in 1803, became a grand duchy in 1805 and joined the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1814. In 1817 Friedrich Koenig and Andreas Bauer founded a maker of steam-driven printing presses there.

On 16 March 1945 about 90 per cent of the city was destroyed in 17 minutes by 225 British Lancaster bombers, and a firestorm killed some 5,000 people. Over the next twenty years the historic buildings were carefully reconstructed, at first largely by the women known as Trümmerfrauen. About 130,000 people live in the city, whose dialect is East Franconian. Its rebuilt old town and the Würzburger Residenz are cultural heritage, the Residence being a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
